title: Thread parking latency notes
content:
Context:
Quick scratchpad exploring whether OS thread parking/unparking behavior is contributing to p95/p99 token latency regressions on light-weight inference requests (short prompts, <64 tokens). Noticed spikes correlated with low-util periods and high concurrency churn.

Hypothesis:
- When worker threads enter park state due to idleness, the unpark path (kernel + scheduler) can add 100s of microseconds occasionally.
- Combined with our async I/O handoffs and small batches, this produces jittery tails.

Test harness:
- Binary: ./bench/parking_probe (small harness linking to runtime scheduling API)
- Workload: synthetic single-token generation, 8ms model CPU time emulated, 64B payload.
- Platform: dev-x1 (4xA100-ish), kernel 6.1, cgroup v2, cpu-isolation off
- Runner: 120s runs, 30s warmup, sampling at 10k reqs/sec pulse and then a quiet 30s window to observe park/unpark.
- Tools: perf record (sched:sched_wakeup), eBPF tracepoints to timestamp park/unpark, and custom latency collector.

Commands used:
- ./bench/parking_probe --qps 10000 --concurrency 256 --model-sim 8ms --run 120
- sudo perf record -e sched:sched_wakeup -a -g -- ./bench/parking_probe ...

Key findings (raw):
- Median: 3.7ms (stable)
- p95: 6.9ms (small)
- p99: 23.4ms (long tail spikes, ~0.4% requests)
- Observed park/unpark latency spikes aligning with p99 samples: wake latency range 200us - 12ms, bimodal near 300us and ~8-12ms.
- Spike correlation: happens when a worker thread had been idle > 10ms and then new request queued.

Notes on measurement caveats:
- perf sampling introduces overhead; eBPF timestamps used to confirm magnitude.
- Some p99s also correspond to CPU stealing reported in dmesg on one node — need to repro on isolated cores.
- cgroup period/quota can affect scheduler wake patterns (we were on bursts allowed).

Quick experiments run:
1) Pinned worker threads to isolated cores (taskset + NOHZ_FULL tweak): p99 dropped to ~9.8ms, but still above median.
2) Keep-alive spin-for-handoff: when worker spins in short loop before parking (spin 50us), p99 improved to ~7.1ms, at cost of ~0.06% CPU increase.
3) Increase pool warmup threshold (retain threads idle < 100ms): reduces frequency of long wakes, p99 ~8.2ms.
4) Switch to using futex-based handoff (we currently rely on std::condition_variable): marginal improvement ~10%.

Preliminary conclusion:
- Thread parking is a measurable contributor to tail latency for small/light requests. 2 main modes: cheap wakes (~200-500us) and expensive wakes (several ms) when the thread has fully parked and kernel scheduler reschedules on different CPU or when CPU was descheduled.
- Spinning for a short duration before parking is an effective mitigation for our workload given the traffic patterns (short bursts). It trades small steady-state CPU for much better p99.

Proposed next steps:
- Run a controlled A/B on a staging fleet with: (A) baseline, (B) spin-for-50us, (C) pinned-cores + reduced park. Measure cost delta and p99 under real traffic.
- Add eBPF live traces in Canary for 48h to track park/unpark distributions.
- Evaluate kernel cmdline knobs (nohz_full, rcu_nocbs) in dedicated node images (requires infra coord).
- Consider a configurable runtime option: thread-warmth (spin window ms) with default 50us and safe guard to disable on cost centers.

Open questions / TODOs:
- What is customer-visible cost tradeoff? compute the CPU delta vs token cost for hosted API.
- Are there scenarios (multi-tenant noisy neighbors) where spinning worsens throughput due to contention? Need multi-tenant sims.
- Validate across CPUs (Intel/AMD) and kernels (5.15 vs 6.1).

Quick action items (who):
- Nora: run A/B on staging with spin=50us and collect p50/p95/p99 (JIRA INF-2987)
- Hao: bake eBPF trace collector for park/unpark and add to canary (GH PR above)
- Lysander (me): prototype a runtime flag and perf-test interactions with batching logic.

Notes-to-self: keep this doc lightweight. Save full traces under gdrive:shared_drives/engineering/serving-runtime/benchmarks/parking_traces/ (manual).

End of note.
